implementation_notes: Python has no standard-library object pool, but the local idiom needs no class hierarchy: pre-fill a queue.LifoQueue with instances (maxsize bounds the pool), take one with get() and return it with put() in a finally, and wrap that in a contextmanager so callers write `with pool.acquire() as obj:` - LIFO reuse keeps the hottest instances hot. The queue module's own locking makes the pool thread-safe, and get(block=..., timeout=...) / get_nowait() with queue.Empty are the exhaustion policy. For database connections the dominant framework realisation is SQLAlchemy's QueuePool (pool_size, max_overflow, pool_recycle, pool_timeout), which deliberately creates connections lazily on first checkout rather than pre-creating them.
pitfalls: A finally block that forgets put() loses the instance silently - the pool shrinks until every caller blocks in get(); broken connections must be discarded and replaced, not returned.
Pre-filling with maxsize means a slow factory at start-up; if instances are cheap, create lazily on first checkout the way SQLAlchemy's QueuePool does.
The queue keeps pooled objects alive, so references they hold (sessions, big buffers) stay reachable - clear per-client attributes on release or the pool becomes a memory leak.
